title: PS-17 Evaluation of different methods to determine pregnancy in beef cattle
content:
Abstract
Determination of pregnancy is a routine practice for many cattle producers post breeding as a checkpoint to their herds reproductive health. Pregnancy determination is generally completed via manual rectal palpation, rectal ultrasound palpation, or blood testing. Depending on the age of the expected fetus and status of bull removal, each method having advantages and/or disadvantages. Blood testing and ultrasounding are considered less invasive and more favorable at detecting early pregnancies (less than 45-days). Blood tests can detect pregnancy in the bovine female as early as 25 days or more after conception whereas ultrasound is successful 30 days or greater post conception. While detecting pregnancy as early as possible is ideal, blood testing for pregnancy in large commercial herds is commonly time consuming, labor intensive, and costly. Typically, ultrasounding reveals quicker results and is less labor intensive. In this study, the herd sires remained with the breeding age females up to the day of pregnancy determination and all cows (n=120) were ultrasounded by an experienced (non-DVM) ultrasound professional using an EVOII ultrasound unit equipped with an eCLi4 3-7 MHz curved rectal probe. Any cow determined non-pregnant (open) with the ultrasound unit had approximately 3 ml of blood collected via the coccygeal vein. The collected blood samples were transported to the Texas Veterinary Medical Diagnostic Lab (TVMDL) in Canyon, Texas where they were tested for Pregnancy Specific Binding Protein (PSBP). Ninety-two (92) or 76.7% of the cows were confirmed pregnant via ultrasound (fetus visible on the ultrasound monitor). Twenty-eight (28) or 23.3% of the cows were deemed non-pregnant via ultrasound. Therefore, blood samples were collected on those called open cows. Of the twenty-eight (28) collected blood samples, seven (7) or 25.0% were confirmed pregnant, four (4) or 14.3% were classified as rechecks and seventeen (17) or 60.7% were confirmed open based on the PSBP levels. In conclusion, this study suggests beef cattle producers should remove all breeding sires from the herd at least 30-d prior to ultrasound or blood testing for pregnancy.
